cards.front: Define the coordinate vector of a vector $v$ with respect to a basis $B = \{b_1, \dots, b_n\}$.
cards.back: The coordinate vector $[v]_B$ is the unique column vector of scalars $\begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ \vdots \\ c_n \end{bmatrix}$ such that $v = c_1 b_1 + \dots + c_n b_n$.

We need to find $c_1, c_2$ such that $c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$. This forms the system:
$$ \begin{cases} c_1 + 3c_2 = 7 \\ 2c_1 + c_2 = 4 \end{cases} $$
Solving, we get $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 2$. Thus, $[v]_B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

cards.front: What is the change-of-basis matrix $P_{C \leftarrow B}$ and how are its columns formed?
cards.back:
The change-of-basis matrix $P_{C \leftarrow B}$ transforms coordinate vectors from basis $B$ to basis $C$. If $B = \{b_1, \dots, b_n\}$ and $C = \{c_1, \dots, c_n\}$, its columns are the coordinate vectors of the basis vectors of $B$ with respect to basis $C$: 
$$ P_{C \leftarrow B} = \left[ [b_1]_C \ [b_2]_C \ \dots \ [b_n]_C \right] $$

cards.front: State the formula relating $[v]_C$ to $[v]_B$ using the change-of-basis matrix $P_{C \leftarrow B}$.
Let $B = \{b_1, \dots, b_n\}$ and $C = \{c_1, \dots, c_n\}$ be bases. Express $P_{C \leftarrow B}$ in terms of $P_B$ and $P_C$, where $P_B$ maps from $B$ to the standard basis $E$.
cards.back:
Let $E$ be the standard basis. We know that $[v]_E = P_B [v]_B$ and $[v]_E = P_C [v]_C$. 
From the first equation, $[v]_B = P_B^{-1} [v]_E$ (if $P_B$ is invertible, which it is for a basis). 
Substitute $[v]_E$ from the second equation into the first: $P_C [v]_C = P_B [v]_B$. 
Multiplying by $P_C^{-1}$ on the left, we get: $[v]_C = P_C^{-1} P_B [v]_B$. 
By definition, $P_{C \leftarrow B}$ is the matrix such that $[v]_C = P_{C \leftarrow B} [v]_B$. 
Therefore, $P_{C \leftarrow B} = P_C^{-1} P_B$. (Here $P_B = [b_1 \dots b_n]$ and $P_C = [c_1 \dots c_n]$).

cards.front: How are the change-of-basis matrices $P_{C \leftarrow B}$ and $P_{B \leftarrow C}$ related?
cards.back:
They are inverses of each other: $P_{B \leftarrow C} = (P_{C \leftarrow B})^{-1}$.
This is because if you transform coordinates from $B$ to $C$ using $P_{C \leftarrow B}$, then transforming them back from $C$ to $B$ using $P_{B \leftarrow C}$ must restore the original coordinates. So, $P_{B \leftarrow C} P_{C \leftarrow B} = I$ (the identity matrix).

Let $b_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $b_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$. We need to find $[b_1]_C$ and $[b_2]_C$.
For $[b_1]_C$: Solve $c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$. This gives $c_1 = 1$ and $c_1+c_2=0 \Rightarrow 1+c_2=0 \Rightarrow c_2=-1$. So $[b_1]_C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$.
For $[b_2]_C$: Solve $c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$. This gives $c_1 = 1$ and $c_1+c_2=2 \Rightarrow 1+c_2=2 \Rightarrow c_2=1$. So $[b_2]_C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
Therefore, $P_{C \leftarrow B} = \left[ [b_1]_C \ [b_2]_C \right] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$.
